Unless you people have seen different information than I have, you
are blowing these events entirely out of proportion for at least two reasons.
1: WotC is not DISCONTINUING their role-playing games. It is true that they
will no longer be the ones creating and manufacturing the games, but the
games will still be around, even if you have to buy them from a new company.
2: WotC may be letting go of 30 employees, but, given the number of employees
that they've hired over the past two years, it seems to be an insignificant
number. I know that doesn't help the employees, but if you boycotted a
product every time the company laid off workers, you would never buy
anything.

I personally think that this is the right move for WotC. Since
Magic started, they have never been able to keep up with demand for their
COLLECTIBLE-TRADING CARD GAME BASED products. By focusing the company solely
on these products, they stand a much better chance of meeting demands and
issuing higher quality products. I don't know about you, but I look forward
to a more efficient company at the head of Jyhad/V:tes production.

Messages.Body:
In message <4a9ku8$m...@cville-srv.wam.umd.edu>, MalKAViaN said:
> Unless you people have seen different information than I have, you
> are blowing these events entirely out of proportion for at least two reasons.
> 1: WotC is not DISCONTINUING their role-playing games. It is true that they
> will no longer be the ones creating and manufacturing the games, but the
> games will still be around, even if you have to buy them from a new company.

I'll believe it when I see it. Also, it doesn't really matter--this
was a company that spent a great deal of time claiming it was
interested in continuing to give something to the RPG community.
Meanwhile, the company was planning on axing these lines to focus
on the bottom line. One doesn't need to specialize like that
to create a good CCG--look at SJG/INWO. I haven't seen GURPS
axed yet...

I also wonder how likely some of these roleplaying games are to get
snapped up--given the CCG craze, buying up an old RPG is just not
as profitable as it once was. And by the time CCGs die (or fade
to a more reasonable level) it will likely be too late for Ars
Magica and Everway.

> 2: WotC may be letting go of 30 employees, but, given the number of employees
> that they've hired over the past two years, it seems to be an insignificant
> number. I know that doesn't help the employees, but if you boycotted a
> product every time the company laid off workers, you would never buy
> anything.

I hold RPG/gaming companies to a different standard than I do,
for example, Pepsi or Sony or whatever. This is a cottage industry,
one T$R in the industry is enough (and no, I don't buy from them,
either.)

More to the point, it is beyond sleazy
to do this 2 weeks before Christmas. I don't care what your
motives are--if you care a whit about your employees, you don't
pull shit like that. It's disgusting. And with no warning--
the *day* *before* the announcement, WotC was going along like
nothing had changed--no slowdown, no warning that this might have
been in the works. Just *boom*--30 people out their jobs.

> I personally think that this is the right move for WotC.

It's an abysmally stupid move. Magic will die. It's in the
process of doing so. Most of the people who play it are kids,
who will find the next fad, stop buying, etc. Sales at the local
level are already slipping (by anecdotal evidence--my local gaming
store manager, and the posted anecdotes of other folks in the
rec.games.frp hierarchy), and that will soon impact new orders,
if it hasn't already. By putting all of their energy into what
is, in the short term, the most profitable product at the expense
of diversifying into different fields makes one that much more
susceptible to the failure of that one field.

> Since
> Magic started, they have never been able to keep up with demand for their
> COLLECTIBLE-TRADING CARD GAME BASED products. By focusing the company solely
> on these products, they stand a much better chance of meeting demands and
> issuing higher quality products. I don't know about you, but I look forward
> to a more efficient company at the head of Jyhad/V:tes production.

Ha. V:TES is next. (unless it's significantly more popular
than I realize, which is always a possibility)

-c

Messages.Author: Colin Bunnell
Messages.Body:
Well, Wizards of the Coast has made its last dollar from me
(who has sunk a significant amount of money into this
game and had planned on continuing to do so.) With the
announcement that they have axed all RPG products,
including Ars Magica, and some 30 employees--2 weeks before Christmas, no
less--Wizards of the Coast has confirmed that they hold
none of the tenets they once held as a corporation, and
that collectible card games are a more significant threat
to RPGs than I was previously willing to believe. My
first love is to RPGs (the route by which I was attracted
to Jyhad and Magic), and to see a company completely
divest itself from RPGs (including one of the best
I've ever come across--Ars Magica. Eagerly did I await
the 4th edition. Pity.) to focus all efforts on Magic:
the Cash Cow is disappointing. Unless this all turns out
to be someone's idea of a really bad joke, you've lost
another customer.

-c

Messages.Body:
In message <4aipp7$5...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>, Thomas R Wylie said:

> We intend to contiue to give something to the *gaming* community. This
> includes accepting that we are not prepare to do enough justice to our
> RPGs to warrant hanging onto them, when we could hand them off to someone
> more interested in developing them - just as White Wolf handed off
> Ars Magica to us, for example.

I can accept that, except for the suddenness of the decision, and
the idiotic way in which Ars Magica was handled. Disclaimer: I am
a newcomer to the game--I just recently bought the 3rd edition, and
discovered a really terrific game contained therein. Now, having spent
the time since then reading about how 4th edition would be coming out,
and how snazzy it was going to be, well, I was looking forward to that.
Now, you all have spent the money to acquire AM, you have spent the
money to develop AM4, you were almost all ready to go to press, and....
is it any wonder your president said "we've never turned a profit on
an RPG"?

> SJG has been doing RPGs for several years, and then jumped into/flirted
> with the TCG market. They are definitely much better equipped to develop
> and RPG than we are.

Again, I accept that you all can't handle an RPG. Fine.
The manner in which the decision was made sucks, though, and
it demonstrates why TCGs are a threat to RPGs--these RPGs
may well find good homes. But they (barring being acquired
by SJG, WW, or T$R) will not be acquired by a company whose
name carries as much clout, and therefore the games will suffer.
I would be surprised (very pleasantly) if AM4 ever sees light of
day, quite frankly. And that saddens me.

> >More to the point, it is beyond sleazy

> >to do this 2 weeks before Christmas...
> An accident of the timing of the budget review process.

You were required, then, to axe all of these people *NOW*?

> Examining
> expenses is what led to this; if we reviewed the budgets during the
> summer, all of this would have happened during the summer. By doing
> this *now*, we give people that much of a head start in finding new
> employment, either here or elsewhere.

*guffaw* uh-huh. The concept of a transition period ever occur
to anyone? The possibility that WotC might tell people "Within
the next 6 months we're divesting from RPGs. Prepare accordingly."
Put out AM4 (since you've spent so much money on its development,
might as well give it a little time to make a little money) Or
don't, but continue to entertain offers during that time, find
the 'good home' you're looking for, and work to see to it that
the games don't suffer, since you want to "give back to the gaming
community."

Not that it matters now, it's a bit late. But WotC has consistently
shown itself to be less concerned as a corporation with the
opinions of its customers (read: VtES Card backs) than it should
be, and that has cost the corp. another customer. I sort of look
forward to the howls here on r.g.t-c.j when you all axe VtES.

-c

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
MalKAViaN <naz...@wam.umd.edu> wrote:
> Unless you people have seen different information than I have, you
>are blowing these events entirely out of proportion for at least two reasons.
>1: WotC is not DISCONTINUING their role-playing games. It is true that they
>will no longer be the ones creating and manufacturing the games, but the
>games will still be around, even if you have to buy them from a new company.

Essentially correct. All discontinued products will continue to be available;
we just won't be producing any new RPGS, for example, for a while. We are
also looking for new homes for all of our RPG lines. It's not that we don't
like RPGS, or don't want RPGs to continue, or that we don't like any of
our RPGs... it's just that we feel that our energies are better spent
elsewhere, and that they'd benefit more from a new home. While the company
was originall formed to produce RPGs, it's clear that our focus has drifted
away from that.

>2: WotC may be letting go of 30 employees, but, given the number of employees
>that they've hired over the past two years, it seems to be an insignificant
>number. I know that doesn't help the employees, but if you boycotted a
>product every time the company laid off workers, you would never buy
>anything.

I wouldn't call roughly 10% of our workforce insignficant :) but there
are a couple of things that people are probably overlooking here. First,
between severance pay and profit sharing decks, all of these employees
have until at least February before they need to start worrying about finances.
Second, in most or all cases we didn't lay off the people; we laid off the
positions. I imagine at least a few of them will ultimately be rehired
into other positions.

> I personally think that this is the right move for WotC. Since
>Magic started, they have never been able to keep up with demand for their
>COLLECTIBLE-TRADING CARD GAME BASED products. By focusing the company solely
>on these products, they stand a much better chance of meeting demands and
>issuing higher quality products. I don't know about you, but I look forward
>to a more efficient company at the head of Jyhad/V:tes production.

Yes, the moves are definitely to let us focus better on trading card games.
Note that it is to focus on *all* of our trading card games, including
VTES, Netrunner, and any future games; the change was not just so we could
focus more on Magic.

Does anyone here play Robo Rally? I ask this because it is the only WotC game
I've played besides M:tG and Jyhad/V:TES. In my opinion, Robo Rally is
manufactured with the highest quality I've ever seen in a board game. The
pieces look great and mine at least had no defects. The cards and boards look
exceptional. Despite having some potentially confusing rules, I found the
rulebook was not only attractive but clearly written, and I learned the rules
very quickly and easily by reading the book. I have never played their RPG's,
but from what everybody is saying they were made with the same exceptional
level of quality.

When it comes to their CCG's, everyone complains about the quality, though.
"This card spoils the game." "There are too many misprints." "They take too
long to put out expansions." "They are greedy and just kick out expansions as
fast as they can, too fast to make a quality product." However, their other
games show us that they do quality work. I think that the difference is that
CCG's are a whole different bucket of fish. I think there is more to
producing a CCG than many of us realize. It is inherently difficult to
produce cards that can push or even break the rules without breaking the game.
I think there is also a hell of a lot more playtesting needed for a CCG than
for any other game. Every new card developed has to be considered in
combination with every other card ever made, to see if it will break the game.
The thing we forget, though, is that CCG's have to be pushed rapidly through
the design process. It may or may not be true, but the opinion of most CCG
players is that a CCG gets stale if it doesn't get an expansion soon enough.
If you don't believe me, just read all the posts complaining about how long it
took for DS to come out.

The point is, WotC's other games have shown that they produce quality
products. I think slamming them because of some misprints in their CCG's is
hasty judgement, and ignores the special circumstances involving the CCG
market. It is my opinion that WotC has done remarkably well with their CCG's.
We all know that Magic has its problems, but then again, it was the FIRST game
of its type, and for all its problems, it is still the favorite CCG to date.
And I don't think anyone here will disagree that Jyhad is the closest game to
being completely balanced without need of card limits.

What it all boils down to is I enjoy the games they make, and everyone here
must at least enjoy Jyhad/V:TES too, or why would they bother to read this
group? Perhaps we can have less "Die WotC, die!" and "Kill Tom!" here, and
get on to enjoying the game, and maybe positively discussing what will best
make this game as balanced as possible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dave Andrews
S2...@nmu.edu
